# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## The Old Model of Toughness

College students described toughness as "hard-nosed," "gritty," "playing through pain," "stoic." Among 160 elite athletes, "perseverance" topped the list. The traditional image: a football player popping a dislocated shoulder back in, Craig MacTavish (last NHL player without a helmet), a wounded military hero, or a mother fighting through discomfort for her child. When toughness is mentioned, many picture a strong brute of a man. Bobby Knight exemplified this model—over 900 wins, three NCAA championships, 1976 perfect season (undefeated, sweeping the tournament). He defined toughness as "Being able to overcome obstacles. You can't feel sorry for yourself." His 1976 team pioneered a pressing man-to-man defense requiring discipline, work ethic, and perseverance. But his methods included tampons hung in lockers of "soft" players, tirades ("This is absolute fucking bullshit. Now I'll fucking run your ass right into the ground"), toilet paper with feces, and choking a player. Knight's version: showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, using fear.

## Parenting and Callousness

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind classified parenting by responsiveness and demandingness. Responsiveness: "the extent to which parents intentionally foster individuality, self-regulation, and self-assertion by being attuned, supportive, and acquiescent to children's special needs and demands." Demandingness: "the claims parents make on children to become integrated into the family whole, by their maturity demands, supervision, disciplinary efforts and willingness to confront the child who disobeys." Three categories: permissive (low demandingness, high responsiveness), authoritarian (high demandingness, low responsiveness), and authoritative (high demandingness, high responsiveness—the "just right" fit). Authoritarian parents rely on fear, threats, punishment—"You need to do this because I said so." In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should "love their child unconditionally." 81% of Americans thought parents too soft. Baumrind's principles apply beyond parenting: we have taken the demanding part and forgotten warmth, care, and responsiveness.

The language of toughness reveals confusion: "soft," "hardening up," "man up," "stop being a pussy." Callous means to harden, make insensitive, develop thick skin. In youth sports, we send kids to run laps or burpees not for training adaptation but to "toughen them up." As Mark Hyman reported in *Until It Hurts*, parents justified teaching eleven-year-olds to go until they puke: "The stern approach is necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior." As *A League of Their Own* summarized: "There's no crying in baseball!" Masculinity is ingrained—more The Rock or Vin Diesel than a small female. Women, who research shows handle pain better, may have the correct definition all along.

## The Downfall of Callous Toughness

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair, 19, showed signs of heatstroke during conditioning (ten 110-yard sprints). He bent over, cramped, but coaches yelled "get him the [expletive] up" and "drag his [expletive] across the field." It took 34 minutes to remove him from the field, another 28 to call 911—1 hour 28 minutes total. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke. Rhabdomyolysis cases from extreme workouts have increased. As Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath described, these workouts aim to "toughen up the current players or weed out a few."

Punishment and expectations aren't inherently bad. The problem arises when demandingness far outweighs support, creating an authoritarian style. Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggression, substance abuse. In sport, it's linked to lower grit, emotional exhaustion, burnout, fear of failure. In one study of over 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting linked to higher child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, those from authoritarian environments coped worse. Ironically, this approach creates fragile, dependent individuals. As the author writes, proclaiming old-school toughness is like declaring the best way to teach swimming is to throw every kid into the deep end. One young athlete explained: "Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger... I need to work harder because I don't want to be punished."

## Redefining Toughness

Real toughness: "experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It's navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can." Fake toughness is control-driven, fear-based, fueled by insecurity, appearance over substance—it creates fragility and responding out of fear. Real toughness provides the tool set to handle adversity; it's about working with your body and mind instead of against them, requiring many tools, not just a hammer.

Pete Carroll—one of only three coaches to win both NCAA championship and Super Bowl—believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges. He encourages meditation, yoga, ring toss when players get heated. "Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they've been prepared to do." Other successful coaches: Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, Mike D'Antoni ("We keep it positive here"). As Ken Reed summarized: "For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach."

In 2008, researchers studied nearly 200 basketball players and concluded: "The 'keys' to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach's ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service."

The military, often seen as the epitome of demanding toughness, has actually been perfecting this other model of resilience for decades. As the source notes, we took the drill sergeant but forgot the training and support.

## The Author's Journey

The author collapsed during a mile race at Cal's Don Bowden Mile (first American to break four minutes in 1957). His strategy was to zone out, turn his brain off for the first half, then reengage for the final lap. At 900 meters, he felt a high-pitched gasping sensation—his breathing, always reliable, suddenly malfunctioned. Panic set in: "What was that? What's wrong? It's over." He tried pushing through, but within 100 meters he couldn't breathe and collapsed. He had paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—vocal cords shut on inhalation. The mechanism: the vocal cords become hyperresponsive, ready to shut at any moment like a trigger-happy guard. Diagnosed by Dr. Stephen Miles. The American Thoracic Society cites "strong emotions" and stress as triggers. The author's old strategy—pushing until he puked—backfired, exacerbating the issue. He had to learn to relax, keep breathing and mind steady, at the moment of maximum discomfort. This search led to the four pillars: ditch the facade, embrace reality; listen to your body; respond instead of react; transcend discomfort.

# Chapter 10: Build the Foundation to Do Hard Things

## The Cultlike Environment

Julie, a college freshman, experienced a coach who commanded "Don’t talk to them. They’re your competitor, your enemies." The coach posted ranked lists, made remarks about weight ("Sex makes you gain weight"), and created "us against the world" mentality. Julie reflects: "It’s almost like we were in a cult." Research identifies four elements of controlling leaders: controlling use of rewards, negative conditional regard, intimidation and isolation, excessive personal control.

## Inner Drive vs. External Control

A meta-analysis covering over 120 years found less than 2% overlap between salary and job satisfaction. A Gallup study of over 1.4 million employees found no relationship between engagement and pay. People motivated by inner drive are three times more engaged. In a study of over 100 British athletes, inner drive led to better persistence, seeing challenges instead of threats, positive coping strategies.

Reengagement is vital: on Everest, of climbers who reached the death zone (over 8,000 meters), only 10% died going up, while 73% perished on the way down. Autonomous motivation allows shifting goals when needed.

## Self-Determination Theory

Edward Deci and Richard Ryan's self-determination theory (SDT) identifies three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence, relatedness. John Mahoney's PhD research on over 200 runners and rowers found satisfying these needs related to toughness and improved racing times. The social environment (coach) played a large role.

Erica Carleton and Mark Beauchamp studied 57 NBA head coaches (2000-2006). Abusive leadership (ridicule, blame) led to a drop in player efficiency scores and increased technical fouls throughout the player's entire career. Paper title: "Scarred for the Rest of My Career?"

## Support, Progress, Belonging

Steve Kerr, coach of Golden State Warriors, handed coaching duties to players Andre Iguodala and Draymond Green during a 44-13 season. "It’s the players’ team. They have to take ownership." In a study of 64 NCAA track teams, servant leadership led to higher mental toughness and faster times. Among over 1,000 office workers, the strongest predictor of handling demanding work was feeling respected by managers.

Psychological safety was the top characteristic of good teams in Google's two-year study. Michael Kraus, Cassey Huang, and Dacher Keltner tracked NBA players' fist bumps, high fives, and positive interactions—teams with more such signals performed better. Gregg Popovich's Spurs had three-hour team meals with no agenda. Military research found bonds built during "noncombat time—the hours of nothingness, the shared boredom."

Dan Coyle's vulnerability loop: trust requires vulnerability first. Maslow's hierarchy originally had self-transcendence as the highest rung, not self-actualization. He wrote that "most industrialists will carefully conceal their idealism... under a mask of toughness."

# Chapter 11: Find Meaning in Discomfort

## Viktor Frankl's Three Ways to Meaning

Viktor Frankl, MD/PhD, delivered lectures in 1946 on meaning. Three ways: doing (creating), experiencing (nature, love, art), and suffering. "True suffering of an authentic fate is an achievement, and, indeed, is the highest possible achievement." Frankl had visualized giving this lecture while in a concentration camp. His manuscript was confiscated at Theresienstadt in 1942. He lost his mother, father, and wife. He wrote *Man's Search for Meaning* in nine days.

## Purpose as Fuel

Performance = Actual effort / Expected Effort × Drive. The body never reaches zero reserves; drive determines how close to empty we can push. Purpose acts as a turbo boost. Frankl observed phases in camp: shock (flirting with suicide via electric fence), then apathy ("Hmm" at death). Survival depended on inner freedom: "It was essential that we should die a death of our own and not the death that the SS had forced on us!"

Research on 89 Holocaust survivors (Katarzyna Prot-Klinger) highlighted support, belonging, having someone to return to, preserving normalcy, luck. Aaron Antonovsky found coherence (comprehensibility, manageability, meaningfulness) mattered. Post-traumatic growth (PTG) studies on Vietnam POWs: longer captivity, more physical injuries, higher growth. As psychiatrist Adriana Feder stated: "Severe trauma triggers a search for meaning and a fundamental reconfiguration of a person’s life goals."

## The Author's OCD

The author has suffered from OCD since childhood—rituals like touching doorknobs front and back, turning alarm on/off seven times. Thought-action fusion: thinking a terrible thought feels as bad as doing it. Research shows OCD brains struggle to learn what's safe; the prefrontal cortex doesn't fire safety signals. The author learned to create space between thought and action, recognizing that "a thought is a thought, and some are meaningless."

## Real Toughness

Real toughness is acceptance: of who you are, what you're facing, the discomfort. It's living in nuance and complexity. As biographer Joshua Wolf Shenk wrote of Lincoln: "He did not pretend to be anything other than he was." Be who you are. That's real toughness.
